A system of linked canals in eastern China, joining the Yangtze valley in the south to the Yellow River plain and later to Beijing in the north. It is the longest artificial waterway in the world, and for 1,300 years it carried the grain that fed China's capitals.

Shorter canals existed long before, some dug in the 5th century BCE. The Sui dynasty joined them into one network in the early 600s. Emperor Yang drove huge gangs of forced labourers to finish it in a few years, one reason his dynasty fell.

Why it mattered:

  • After the period of division, the south grew most of China's rice, but the capitals and armies sat in the north. The canal moved the tax grain between them.
  • It tied the two halves of the country together politically as well as economically.
  • Merchants, officials and ideas travelled along it, and cities such as Yangzhou and Hangzhou grew rich on it.

The route changed over time. The Yuan cut a more direct line to their capital at Beijing, and the Ming rebuilt it after moving their own capital there in 1421. The current main line runs about 1,776 km from Beijing to Hangzhou. In the 19th century, shifts of the Yellow River and the rise of steamships and railways ended its role as the empire's main artery. Its southern sections still carry barges today.
